However, its sample inefficiency and the difficulty of de-biasing estimates in nonparametric settings have restricted its practicality in many real-world scenarios. Given that causal inference is also known for its sample inefficiency, we investigate if integrating well-established causal methods with modern RL techniques can enhance learning speed. To address this, we introduce a novel online learning algorithm that effectively merges instrumental variable (IV) methods with RL. We prove that this algorithm achieves a regret bound. Extensive experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that our approach not only learns efficient policies but also outperforms existing state-of-the-art IV-RL algorithms in sample efficiency. We further validated these findings using real-world datasets, confirming that our method is applicable to causal impact assessment within bandit frameworks. Overall, this research offers a fresh perspective on accelerating policy learning by leveraging traditional causal inference tools.

Our primary observation is that a wide range of existing causal techniques, typically used for effect estimation, are actually reinforcement learning algorithms. This implies they can achieve near-optimal performance once sufficient data is collected. Therefore, we ask whether these methods can induce an exploration bonus, similar to how UCB functions in multi-armed bandits, thereby enabling better online decision-making. Our contribution is twofold: first, we determine that while direct application of these methods is challenging, we can learn near-optimal policies in linear contextual bandits with confounding by utilizing instrumental variables and the gradient descent fitting of outcome models—a standard procedure in causal inference. Second, under instrument validity and other mild assumptions, we prove that our algorithm incurs regret only slightly higher than conventional IV-based reward estimation in sample-efficient settings. The core mechanism of our approach is straightforward: since IV methods are fundamentally reinforcement learning algorithms, we can fit outcome models to estimate value functions, followed by applying an $\epsilon$-greedy policy.

The equation's structure mirrors that of the hydrodynamic momentum balance, but the effective mobility includes a divergent contribution analogous to kinematic viscosity in hydrodynamics. This finding suggests the existence of an intrinsic, self-generated scale of inhomogeneity in active nematics, independent of thermal fluctuations or geometric constraints. The divergence stems from the nonreciprocal nature of energy injection and dissipation: inhomogeneities dissipate anisotropy frictionally near their centers, while anisotropy is injected ballistically at boundaries away from the center. This dissipation is nonreciprocal because the state at a point $p$ depends on the orientation of a active molecule at $p$, whereas the orientation field at $p$ does not depend on the state of the molecule at $p$. We validate this divergence quantitatively using a continuum model and two standard atomistic models. Furthermore, by reformulating the order parameter equation in a kinematic viscosity regime, we demonstrate that it takes a form closely resembling the standard parabolic dynamical equation. In this framework, the kinematic viscosity is proportional to the active stress, offering a direct link between the magnitude of the divergence and the strength of activity. Finally, we discuss potential generalizations to other active systems and experimental methods for measuring the divergence and its dependence on the source of broken reciprocity. Our results provide fundamental insight into the characteristic length scales of nonequilibrium active matter systems. [This work is dedicated to the memory of Michael Shelley.]

In this system, disk photoevaporation driven by stellar high-energy radiation has created a gap at a orbital radius of approximately 15–20 au. Our analysis indicates that photoevaporation models predict the strongest free-free signals, arising from a collimated ion wind emanating from the photoevaporated disk surface. This signal could potentially be detected using the VLA in basel modes 22C, 22D, and 22C-5, assuming the disk mass is less than 0.1 solar masses. We advise that a simultaneous observation of the free-free line at 4.86 GHz could help determine the disk mass and mass accretion rate by measuring the free-free opacity. Furthermore, a correlation analysis of free-free emission across different baselines could reveal the spatial structure of the photoevaporated surface or accretion disk. of Federated Learning (FL). Recently, Federated Distillation (FD) has emerged as a novel FL paradigm characterized by distinct communication dynamics. FD utilizes ensemble distillation, enabling the aggregation of model updates over multiple distillation intervals, which substantially reduces communication frequency. Furthermore, FD facilitates the incremental training of heterogeneous client architectures, such as mobile devices with varying computational and memory capacities. Although FD demonstrates potential despite the vulnerabilities introduced by communication constraints, a theoretical understanding of these limitations within its specific context remains absent. This study presents an analysis of the fundamental communication limitations in Federated Distillation. Specifically, it derives exact convergence bounds for the ensemble distillation approach. These bounds illustrate the equilibrium between communication frequency and model performance under heterogeneous conditions. The resulting theoretical findings offer a framework for evaluating emerging FL methodologies with diverse architectural structures. Numerical experiments confirm the validity of these bounds. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for analyzing the communication challenges inherent in federated distillation systems. Key contributions include: (i) an exact convergence bound for FD, (ii) insights into the trade-off between heterogeneous client architectures and communication frequency, and (iii) experimental validation of these bounds. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/Ali-FL-Net/FL_Network_Constraints. In this setting, both reward functions and state transition kernels are unknown and permitted to change arbitrarily over time, subject to a constraint on their cumulative variations. We address this problem using a non-parametric deep reinforcement learning framework based on elastic net regularization. We provide theoretical assurances regarding generalization performance, as well as bounds for regret and regret variance. Our evaluations demonstrate the end-to-end effectiveness of the proposed method, with empirical results indicating its practical efficiency, particularly in scenarios involving small budgets. Additionally, our theoretical analysis is as rigorous as it can be for the non-stationary context, addressing several limitations present in previous studies. This is achieved by introducing a novel variance term to quantify the performance of risk-controlled policies and by developing a sophisticated technique to bound the cumulative error of approximate value function estimates in non-stationary environments. Consequently, our work establishes a balanced and effective approach for learning risk-controlled policies in non-stationary settings, significantly advancing current capabilities in this field. Numerical experiments confirm the validity of our theoretical claims and highlight the distinct advantages of our method over existing approaches.

This documentation approach fosters evolutionary development, allowing issues to be enriched over time, a process that typically culminates in associative metadata like "issue closings." The collaborative nature and incremental structure of knowledge work are frequently overlooked by data science efforts. We aim to investigate these traits and demonstrate their utility. First, we develop and validate methods for "co-analyzing granular collaborative records," which integrate variably timed individual user contributions into a single analysis unit. Second, we introduce techniques for "Co-Analyzing Co-Written Documents," which merge evolving versions of the same document to create a unified analytical unit from collaborative history. Third, we establish methods for "Co-Analyzing Co-Read Documents," which combine documents that users explicitly navigate to and read to form a unified analysis unit. We validate these approaches and prove, for the first time, that co-analyzing co-written documents significantly outperforms standard analytic units when capturing collaborative work. Additionally, we show that co-analysis of co-read documents yields important insights into how users discover and evaluate innovations during collaborative efforts. Our findings are based on 58,889 issues and 158,099 document views analyzed from five major software, video, and hardware companies and one open-source community. While existing research predominantly addresses DML on strict convex objectives with unbounded stochastic gradient noise, this paper focuses on concurrent DML over time-varying networks for general non-smooth and unbounded objective functions. Our proofs rely on constructing an optimistic Lyapunov function and an associated Lyapunov exponent to obtain tighter bounds on noise impacts within DML over time-vary networks. Finally, we validate the theoretical results through extensive numerical experiments.

In recent years, there has been a surge in interest in analyzing the convergence of both centralized and distributed optimization methods. However, most prior research focuses on concurrent updates with bounded noise, yielding a best-case convergence rate of $O(1/T)$. In this work, we demonstrate that a careful re-examination of both centralized and distributed algorithms yields a convergence rate of $O(T^{-\tau})$ for non-smooth and unbounded objectives, where $\tau \in (\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ is determined by the strong convexity parameter of the objective. This improvement over the best prior rate is achieved by leveraging the self-concordance of the composite objective in the primal-dual algorithm and a novel handling of unbounded noise in the accelerated method. We consider the high-dimensional Bayesian linear regression model defined as:

$Y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ (1)

where $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ represents the response variable, $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ denotes the design matrix, $\beta \in \varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the parameter of interest, and the error term $\varepsilon$ follows a normal distribution with mean zero and unknown variance, i.e., $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$. The dimension $p$ is assumed to exceed the sample size $n$. This framework finds extensive application in genomics, neuroimaging, and other fields i.

Standard frequentist approaches to this problem typically rely on Lasso [2] and its variants to perform variable selection and estimate parameters. However, from a Bayesian perspective, the prior distribution of $\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ poses a significant challenge. The conventional Lasso prior, an $\ell_1$-regularized Gaussian prior, is improper and fails to constitute a valid probability measure since it does not integrate to one. Consequently, the primary objective of this paper is to propose and examine fully Bayesian procedures for high-dimensional linear regression when the variance $\sigma^2$ is unknown.

This study extends that framework to a system exhibiting Mott insulator superfluid (MIS) instability. By maintaining mobile charge density below the Mott gap and treating charge binding energy within the Mott gap as a tunable parameter, we derive conditions that induce spin and charge separation in the MIS phase. However, current visual exploration methods for large-scale networks remain underdeveloped. To address this need, we introduce NGLNet, a system designed for the interactive 3D visualization and exploration of large biological networks. We demonstrate that if WIMPs interact with nuclear targets inside WDs through inelastic scattering and possess a mass exceeding typical heralding thresholds, their annihilation rate in the core surges following each gamma-ray heralding event. When the WIMP mass falls within the few hundred GeV range and the WD core density reaches several times nuclear saturation density, the energy released during each capture event can reach up to several petaelectronvolts. However, for weakly bound WIMPs such as those produced at the LHC, the released energy is reduced to a fraction of the heralding signal. Should WIMP-nucleus scattering be significant enough to enable core accumulation, this energy release could either thermalize as heat or initiate spallation reactions in the WD's crust. The latter scenario would generate numerous observable MeV gamma rays from crust nuclei photodisintegration and would cause abrupt, large-scale dimming of the WD if spallation occurs in the crust. These novel signatures could facilitate the detection of WIMPs in the challenging sub-100 TeV mass range. Additionally, WIMP accumulation and the resulting energy release could modify the cooling rates of compact stars. In this methodology, the classical oscillator is substituted with a quantum harmonic oscillator, and a question mark operator—functioning as a broken logic gate—is implemented to introduce logical uncertainty regarding the system state. This modification, which does not impede system evolution, is essential for entropy expansion. To demonstrate the model's efficacy, entropy is calculated using a macrostate defined by an "average energy" constraint. Evolution is simulated across microstates, with the quantum harmonic oscillator ejection process and the "?" operator sequentially applied to individual oscillators. Distinct from prior radiative models, the quantum uncertainty inherent in this approach naturally generates a radiation field H(t) rich in indeterminate content, where the specific content of each mode remains unknown. The interaction between oscillators and this field is governed by the quantum nature of the oscillator energy levels, replacing a parameterized "coupling" found in earlier studies. Furthermore, the model can be extended to multi-dimensional systems, such as a 2D quantum harmonic quantum corral resembling a quantum cone. In this scenario, the sum of transverse and longitudinal excitations does not directly determine the excitation level of a connected classical logic gate. Consequently, the quantum uncertainty embedded in the quantum corral gives rise to a radiation field of higher dimensionality. Ultimately, the findings indicate that radiation field models capable of sustaining high entropy for long periods are plausible, hinging on the energy quantum and a broken or fuzzy logical connection to the radiating quantum oscillator. These results bear implications for investigating the arrow of time and the origin of entropy. Additionally, the methodology is compatible with, and can be integrated into, the quantum-entropy bridge model by Hall, and its results may offer a mechanism to address the quantum to classical transition in the context of entropy generation. Finally, the findings align with the notion of a quantum universe.

Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for training machine learning models on distributed, privacy-sensitive, and siloed data. By allowing in situ model training on private data and aggregating global models through secure gradient averaging, FL bridges the gap between centralized learning and stringent privacy requirements. Targeted attacks on machine learning models manipulate input data to force incorrect classifier predictions. Although research into such attacks is well-established for static models, recent advancements in learning interpreters for black-box models have shifted the attack landscape. Now, an attacker need not train a substitute model; they can retrain an interpretation model using a few publicly available data points and outputs to launch attacks. We examine several scenarios of this new attack vector. First, we demonstrate how to craft targeted attacks against a data source by learning an interpreter from a limited sample of labeled points. Second, we show how to attack a black-box model without any labeled points if the source domain already exists as an open dataset. We validate our approach on image classification tasks using ImageNet and CUB-200, confirming that our method significantly outperforms traditional adversarial examples.

A primary method for this sampling is Fisher's hypergeometric sampling scheme, which generates random permutations of a binary matrix with fixed margins; the original and sampled matrices are then compared to identify patterns.

Fixed-margin sampling can be extended by incorporating an error tolerance, a move particularly valuable when margin totals are imperfect estimates of target values or when tolerance is mandated for practical reasons, such as ensuring sample sizes remain close to population sizes. By allowing a deviation within a specified tolerance, the search for patterns becomes more sensitive.

To facilitate pattern detection, we develop efficient algorithms for generating random matrices with margins within a permitted tolerance. We validate the correctness and efficiency of our algorithms through comprehensive simulation studies, successfully detecting various binary patterns. Furthermore, our method for margin sampling is robust, producing asymptotically hypergeometric distributions and achieving excellent normal approximations.

Finally, we apply this sampling approach to a real-world scenario: a Chromosome-SNP association table. Our fully binary association tables reveal structurally distinct clusters, a finding crucial for understanding key features of human genome organization. Notably, our method detected structures in the first chromosomal cluster that previous methodologies failed to identify, while accurately reproducing structures in all other major clusters. All code is accessible via a public GitHub repository. By enabling the sampling of binary matrices with fixed (or nearly fixed) row and column sums, this research opens up new methodologies for pattern detection across a wide range of applications.

While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, as processes grow in complexity, the number of required components increases; for instance, next-to-leading order (NLO) predictions for single-parton data include associated emissions, whereas double-parton predictions demand two such emissions. To resolve these issues, we introduce JAM (Joint Analysis of Montepython), a novel tool designed to combine and interpolate PDFs, decays, and cross-sections from different providers. The name JAM stands for "Joining Any Model." This tool facilitates the combination of NLO building blocks for process predictions, allows for the simultaneous inclusion of associated emissions, and can merge multiple processes to form sum statistics, such as single or double-parton production. Additionally, JAM fits and interpolates process-independent input objects like PDFs and decays. Designed for full compatibility with existing analysis tools, JAM enables a seamless transition from cross-section calculation to fitting, allowing for comparisons against a wide range of predictions and the derivation of parton-level and hadron-level observations. A specific version, MC4NPYF, supports the interface with Monte Carlo generators like PYTHIA 8. Additionally, a Web interface is available for analyzing objects and integrating data, including the creation of interpolated runcards. The complete tool is documented in an accompanying paper. This work reports on the application of the tool to NLO single- and double-parton production. Such applications will be detailed in subsequent publications. The source code is available at https://gitlab.cern/ch/JAM.

### 1. Introduction

Microresonator frequency combs (microcombs) have gained significant attention due to their broad applicability and low cost, stemming from their generation mechanism based on the microresonator's fundamental optical field. Gained prominence after the demonstration of comb combing [1], microcombs are now recognized as having complex spectra comprising multiple equally spaced combs or subcombs [2]. The resulting line spacing is determined by the mode-locking frequency of the pump laser or an integer multiple of it [3]. While mode-locked lasers generally achieve high coherence, pump lasers utilizing electro-optic modulation to establish mode locking often suffer from residual phase noise [4, 5]. Consequently, ensuring that each microcomb line maintains a constant phase relationship with the pump laser is challenging. Although optical phase linking is a common solution to this issue, it often demands additional control equipment and complex feedback loops to modify the laser [6, 7, 8]. Therefore, developing a straightforward method to manage microcomb line spacing while preserving coherence is highly valuable.

In this work, we present a novel approach to microcomb spectral control through parametric seeding using a modulated pump laser. By employing dual-sideband modulation of the pump laser, we achieved the generation of an equidistant microcomb line spectrum. This configuration also allowed us to independently investigate the stability of the microcomb line spacing. Our results demonstrate exact copying of the pump laser's double modulation sideband spacing throughout the microcomb's optical spectrum and indicate that the added broadening to the pump laser's linewidth is negligible. These distinct inequalities arise because the entropy landscape of such dual theories can be represented as a piecewise linear function. We demonstrate the utility of this geometric framework by examining dual theories associated with bulk states that possess a single connected component in their bulk spacetime. Specifically, we establish that the dual quantum theory must satisfy the strong subadditivity constraint $I(A:C)=0$ for specific subsets $A$, a condition that is considerably stronger than the standard strong subadditivity inequality $I(A:C)\geq 0$. Strong subadditivity is inherently a "second-order" property, as it involves the partial derivatives of the entropy; consequently, these exceptional theories can be characterized by a collection of "first-order" constraints on the slopes of the entropy surface. For any bulk state with an arbitrary smooth geometry, we identify the corresponding constraints on the dual quantum theory using the path integral formulation. Notably, this approach clarifies the relationship between the quantum inequalities and the classical positivity conditions on the gravitational Hamilton-Jacowski functional. Beyond the standard strong subadditivity $S(AC)\leq C$, we also derive further inequalities of this type that are satisfied by the dual theory when the bulk state is described by a specific geometric partition. The condition $I(A:C)=0$ is actually a restatement of the standard bulk causality requirement that the entropy surface be smooth and devoid of naked conical singularities. Conversely, the novel inequalities are governed by two distinct types of "forbidden" geometric objects: the first are dual to classical concepts such as the Legendre transform of an entropy surface or "entropic branes," whereas the second are dominated by collections of null geodesics in the bulk, which we term "caustics." Any violation of strong subadditivity by the dual quantum theory can be visually mapped to the presence of a forbidden object within the dual geometry. The term "forbidden" is more appropriate than "dual" for these objects, as their analogs are not necessarily well-defined within the classical gravitational framework. The initial set of forbidden objects includes planes and bounded regions in the bulk, which are linked to bulk causality and holographic information bounds, respectively. The inaugural type of object is also dominated by bulk planes when considered in the context of extended entropy surfaces. We anticipate that the characterization of these forbidden objects will offer a novel perspective on the subtleties surrounding the generalization of strong subadditivity to the quantum regime. In this work, we extend this concept to a broader class of conformal field theories. A conformal field theory is represented by a pair $(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{h})$, where $\mathbb{H}$ is a simply connected half-plane and $\mathbf{h}$ is a collection of holomorphic vector fields and tensor fields. We assume access to independent chi-processes for the real parts of the logarithmic derivatives of univalent holomorphic functions mapping $\mathbb{H}$ onto various domains; these processes serve as the "imaginary part" data. A conformal field theory on a domain $D$ then corresponds to a collection of such $(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{h})$-structures on conformal copies of $D$. Without assuming that these field theories extend conformally to the closure of the domains, we define a conformal field theory on $D$ to be defined on the closure if it can be equipped with $(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{h})$-structures on the closure such that: (1) $\mathbb{H}$ contributes nothing to the theory's data, and (2) the resulting collection of $(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{h})$-structures and chi-processes for logarithmic derivatives of univalent functions on the closure is conformally invariant. If these criteria are met for the closure of an increasing sequence of domains whose union is $D$, the limiting object is a collection of $(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{h})$-structures and chi-processes on $D$. Using this framework, we construct a conformal field theory on the closure of any simply connected domain that contains no boundary turning points and is not a "teardrop" domain (i.e., it is not bijectively conformally equivalent to a domain featuring a single boundary turning point). This is achieved by taking the limit as $r \to \infty$ of the conformal field theory defined on the closure of a domain formed by adding a point $z$ to the domain at a distance $1/r$ from all its boundary points.

This area is fundamentally linked to quantum complexity theory and serves as a potential source of quantum-privileged problems. For years, the field has been driven by the hypothesis that a quantum advantage could be achieved using unentangled photons. However, this goal relied on the unproven assumption that preparing single qubit states is difficult, which is contradicted by the established belief that single qubit state verification is easy. Consequently, it remains unproven. In this work, we ask whether it is possible to verify entangled quantum computation. The answer is yes, though the approach is unconventional. It hinges on an unexpected observation: when the circuit $C$ operates on a specific class of state families, the client need only query $C$ once. This occurs because the security relies on the fact that the quantum data is irreversibly scrambled by $C$, a complexity issue closely related to sampling problems. This result holds significant implications for quantum cryptography. Furthermore, it recovers the quantum cryptography assumption that single qubit state preparation is easy and aligns with recent progress in quantifying the scarcity of "useful" computational basis states. Finally, this approach is universally applicable to any circuit $C$ and can be thought of as a form of "black-box" state verification. The proposed scheme is simple, and our findings may inspire the design of more efficient protocols. This research is dedicated to R. Cleve, R. Cleve, and R. Cleve.

While many current approaches successfully generate morphologically accurate cells, they often produce uniformly distributed cells, a condition absent in typical cell cultures. To train segmentation models capable of handling the complexity and heterogeneity of real cultures, a diverse training set is essential. This study demonstrates that computational models trained via reinforcement learning with either visual or articulatory inputs develop both 3D spatial and state representations. Furthermore, by employing new decoding and manipulation techniques, we reveal that state representations offer distinct advantages over their spatial counterparts in certain contexts. These findings have significant implications for designing navigational and cognitive systems within embodied cognitive and neural systems theory. Notably, the resilience of these representational formats to variations in training procedures, model architecture, and algorithm selection indicates that they likely emerge naturally from learning and interaction, independent of prior innate assumptions. Furthermore, the evidence supporting both representation types within latent spaces of neural network controllers utilized by deep reinforcement learning mirrors the dual 2D/3D neural maps discovered in the mammalian hippocampus, suggesting a strong parallel between our biological system and artificial neural networks used for state-based control. Finally, these results validate emerging principles of efficient coding that prioritize flexibility over precision. By enabling agents to generalize from new environments and layouts with minimal new learning, such principles facilitate robust, real-world robotic applications. Specifically, this work supports the development of zero-shot manipulation and transfer learning techniques for both neural and robotic systems. Abstract. Sound localization and detection (SLD) is a critical capability for audio-based perceptual systems, finding essential applications in autonomous driving, human-computer interaction, and security systems. Recent research has focused on eigen sound, a specific class of audio occurring in isolated locations, such as the movement of vehicle wheels on road surfaces. In this study, we introduce a new dataset and benchmark for eigen sound classification and localization in vehicle transportation scenarios using the EigenSound v2 collection. We provide detailed evaluations of the dataset and compare various machine learning-based SELD solutions. Our experiments demonstrate that the P-AMDANet architecture significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we show that the proposed, simple, and effective SELD solution is approximately five times faster than existing state-of-the-art approaches. Conversely, recent wireless applications have explored the benefits of allowing simultaneous transmission by intentionally managing and even leveraging signal interference. Prominent techniques such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), joint source-channel coding, and compute-and-forward rely on advanced error-correcting codes and signal processing algorithms, often demanding significant computational resources and complex infrastructure. Unlike these existing methods, we propose a novel approach where transmitting nodes voluntarily adopt an interference-aware, consensus-based communication protocol. Experimental results indicate that this consensus-based method can more efficiently resolve disputes than traditional techniques, representing a new paradigm where interference is transformed from a liability into an asset that facilitates consensus. This work was created as a proof of concept for a wireless robot node named COSMIC, which will be featured in a subsequent system paper. In recent years, researchers have increasingly turned to sparsity and low-complexity models to analyze high-dimensional data. Many operations in this domain are defined as the composition of a non-linear sparsity-inducing transform with a linear operator. However, composing functions on manifolds is generally ill-posed. This work introduces a general framework for sparsity-inducing transforms on manifolds, accompanied by an associated proximal algorithm. We detail two specific instances of this method: one utilizing a representation learning approach to train a non-linear operator, and another applying pre-computed geodesic distances on the manifold. We also examine the condition under which convergence to a solution is guaranteed. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through two applications: classifying high-dimensional images and estimating the parameters of a Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process on a sphere. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method is highly effective in both applications.

This study introduces the concept of Manifold Representations with Applications, grounded in the observation that data often resides on or near low-dimensional submanifolds. While many successful learning algorithms have been developed to learn linear operators acting on feature maps, there is generally no theoretical guarantee that the resulting feature map actually lies on a manifold. This paper offers a framework for learning non-linear operators that compose with a manifold-inducing transform. A key contribution is proving that this composition remains valid and that the gradient of the composition can be calculated in finite time, a critical requirement for training manifold-based feature representations. distinct flavors of El Niño—the East Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP)/Modoki types—affect the global mean temperature. This study investigates the spatial temperature patterns associated with these events. The analysis reveals that the temperature anomalies linked to El Niño exhibit a consistent octagonal structure. However, the intensity and distribution of these patterns vary depending on the specific occurrence and the regional distribution of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies within the tropical Pacific. Consequently, the impact of El Niño on the global temperature field is both complex and unpredictable. Contrary to prior assumptions, the emergence of the strongest El Niño temperature pattern does not necessarily follow the maximum sea surface temperature anomaly in the eastern Pacific. Furthermore, significant differences exist regarding temperature patterns related to the two classic classifications of Modoki El Niño. Finally, because not all El Niño episodes display a pronounced third summer temperature pattern, we propose that this third pattern is more accurately characterized as a "Pacific-Scale Temperature Pattern" (PSTP).

Black Holes (MBHs) at the centers of massive galaxies. This study presents a deep, narrow-band HST imaging analysis of the high redshift galaxy SDSSJ141629.53+020111.0 (hereafter GHZ1) at $z$ = 1.54, which hosts a MBH with a mass of $(4\text{--}6) \times 10^8 M_{\odot}$. The initial hypothesis identified the point source within GH1 (the galaxy's dominant stellar component) as the MBH based on previous optical imaging, spectroscopy, and previous IR data. However, a detailed HST multi-band analysis reveals the presence of a second star-forming region (SRC2) located approximately 1.2 kpc from the center, characterized by significant stellar mass, recent activity, and varying evidence of feedback mechanisms. We demonstrate that the young age of SRC2 accounts for the previously unidentified offset source and implies the central bright source is likely a young star cluster rather than a MBH. To align with our findings, we re-analyze other multi-wavelength data, including the most recent HST images of GH1, to re-evaluate the nature of the central source and the location of the MBH. Ultimately, we suggest that future HST observations of GH1 are necessary to definitively determine the true position and nature of its MBH. More broadly, this case study offers critical insights into the risks of misidentifying the elusive central objects hosting MBHs. The placement of MBHs influences key astrophysical processes, such as star formation history, chemical evolution, and the presence of rings or bars. Therefore, our work aims to contribute to the ongoing effort to understand the co-evolution of MBHs and their host galaxies. Data from the F160W filter (near-IR) were not incorporated into this research. While our study represents a pioneering use of extensive HST imaging supported by robust photometric and spectral analysis to address the elusive nature of MBH host galaxy centers, it also establishes a methodology for interpreting the recently released HST True Color catalog for high-z MBH galaxies. Furthermore, we plan to employ a similar approach in conjunction with JWST observations for GH1 and a few other high-z galaxies in an upcoming paper. Comparing our results against limited previous data will help assess the benefits and limitations of integrating IR observations into a comprehensive photometric analysis of these

Although flat bands are well-known in geometrically frustrated structures like the kagome lattice, we demonstrate that they also arise in the hyperbolic lattice, which features negative curvature and sparse connectivity. This sparse connectivity, defined by a high ratio of next-nearest to nearest neighbor hopping, induces an effective flat band through an exactly solvable mechanism. We have numerically investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of this system using the full Hubbard model and the superconducting Hubbard model, employing an exact continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo method. Our findings reveal that, despite its flat band, the system does not exhibit an Mott insulating state at half-filling due to the absence of a truly flat band. Instead, the material displays a finite-density superconducting state when the superconducting coupling is non-zero. These results highlight that spatially nonuniform electronic interactions, such as those from strain or dislocation networks, can generate flat band physics in otherwise non-flat lattices. Consequently, this suggests a new strategy for engineering flat band physics and the associated rich correlated physics in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides, a platform already known for its superconductivity and local negative curvature. Additionally, we have derived an analytical condition for the emergence of the flat band by generalizing the sparse connectivity constraint to graphs with non-positive curvature. Finally, we examine a model of an intrinsically flat band on a Sierpinski gasket lattice, which resembles the hyperbolic lattice but possesses a truly flat band due to its lack of connectivity at antipodal points of the Weyl sphere. The resulting physics of this system mirrors that of a standard square lattice, confirming that flat band effects are contingent upon specific local connectivity patterns. Therefore, flat band physics in both lattices is driven by a unified concept of "forbidden" connectivity. This indicates that flat band systems can be identified through the topological properties of their corresponding connection graphs. More broadly, we establish a rigorous framework for classifying flat band and correlated physics based on the topological and geometric characteristics of the underlying connection graph. This facilitates a direct mapping between topological features of connection graphs and the emergence of flat band physics, offering a new approach to understanding the design of flat band systems for correlated physics through topological geometry. Such a method is not limited to condensed matter systems but is also relevant in other fields, such as quantum information. The general connection between topological geometry and flat band physics

deciphering the mutual dynamics of time series. This research presents an innovative approach to forecasting the future synchronization of two time series. We demonstrate that, provided the series share a dependency, their synchronization can be predicted with high accuracy using a local model that relies solely on the time series data itself. This method surpasses existing approaches, including those based on mutual information, by achieving higher prediction accuracy. The proposed technique is straightforward, highly efficient, and does not require the series to be stationary, making it superior to many current methods. The method's efficacy is verified using both synthetic data and real-world datasets. Additionally, we examine the predictability limits imposed by the intrinsic laws of chaos. Our findings indicate that, provided sufficient data is available, one can achieve accurate forecasts regarding the onset of synchronization or the point where series become too distant for a reliable prediction. This has significant practical implications. Furthermore, we estimate the maximum predictability allowed by the laws of chaos and observe that, in many practical scenarios, a substantial amount of information is lost, rendering precise forecasting of synchronization events impossible. This loss is evident when a series is influenced by another, acts as a channel for mutual information, or when two independent series are mistakenly treated as interdependent. Finally, we estimate the mutual information present in the data. This work introduces a novel method for anticipating synchronization events by leveraging cross-correlation analysis. We anticipate that this approach will be beneficial in various contexts. Specifically, the technique is superior to current methods for determining whether time series are synchronized or too divergent, estimating the amount of mutual information, and predicting synchronization events. Key words: synchronization; cross-correlation; local model; mutual information; non-stationary; local model; predictability; Lyapunov exponent; channel; estimating; estimating. This work introduces a method for predicting synchronization.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing the centrifugal field coupling during dynamic terahertz excitation may enable the temporary regulation of the band gap in materials. Furthermore, we show that spin-rotation coupling and centrifugal field coupling are inherently linked to the centrifugal acceleration experienced by nuclei. This acceleration, which can reach approximately 1,000 ps$^{-2}$, far exceeds the static acceleration of Earth. These effects arise from fundamental fundamental frequencies and structural properties; for instance, the strength of spin-rotation coupling in circularly excited vibrational modes is directly proportional to the centrifugal acceleration of the excited rotating bond. Consequently, tuning molecular or crystalline fundamental frequencies and structural geometries provides precise control over these phenomena. Given that the excited-state energies and circular motion of nuclei alter electronic structure and function on a transient timescale, fundamental frequency and crystal geometry engineering offers a new approach to short-timescale control of central technologies like quantum computing and chemical reactions. These findings present a fresh perspective on manipulating and coupling vibrational and electronic excitations, as well as controlling spin dynamics and crystalline excitations through centrifugal effects. Additionally, the analogies and distinctions between these effects and static, pressure-induced field coupling, along with their potential application to rotational field engineering for central quantum bits, offer a pathway for future research. Finally, the connection between circular ion motion and the geometric phase of electrons introduces topological physics into the study of centrifugal effects. The presence of a centrifugal field in dynamically excited systems expands the scope of physics required to understand and utilize terahertz physics and spectroscopy. We have illustrated these concepts using a vibrational mode of a double bromine molecule (Br$_2$) and the CO$_3^{2-}$ ion. Our methodology is generally applicable to various molecular and crystalline structures and can be extended to other vibrational and electronic excitations. The approach of utilizing centrifugal field coupling to modify excitations complements existing methods such as electric field control (Stark effect), pressure-induced field coupling, and photonic field engineering. Nevertheless, large-scale data fusion presents distinct challenges. This study introduces a novel large-scale data fusion framework designed for rs-fMRI connectivity analysis. First, individual subject connections are learned independently using a regularized optimization approach. Second, a canonical correlation analysis filter is applied to fuse these connections into a group-level representation. Third, the efficiency of this fused connection is evaluated through distributed matrix estimation, which incorporates sampling noise and regularization to produce stable group-level estimates suitable for large-scale analysis. As an application, we derive a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs exhibiting positive Ricci curvature. This study investigates the relationship between character-level language tagging and the underlying linguistic composition (LCUC), defining LCUC as the process of identifying the language for each constituent word within a CM sentence. We frame the problem as unsupervised learning, aiming for a solution that does not rely on training data, thereby avoiding the need for large, monolingual corpora that are often unavailable to end users. Finally, we explore the relationship between LCUC and character-level tagging, demonstrating that character-level predictions can guide the LCUC process. Experimental results indicate a strong correlation between the two, highlighting the utility of this unsupervised solution for improving language identification accuracy. Additionally, we present a analysis of error patterns in both the experimental results and the model's predictions. To our knowledge, this is the first unsupervised BERT-based approach to language identification for CM text. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/RahimatallahB/IC2021_NLI. Fisher introduced the concept of reproductive value, which has historically been viewed as abstract, counterintuitive, and challenging to teach. This work presents an alternative formulation of that theorem, accompanied by a proof based on reproductive _gains_ instead of reproductive value, offering a more accessible approach to the fundamental lemma of evolutionary genetics. Furthermore, by employing a simple vector-based analogy, we demonstrate that reproductive gains can be measured in biological traits that have not yet been stabilized by natural selection. In this context, the analysis of reproductive gains in Heterosis, or heterozygote advantage, becomes more intuitive. We show that if Heterosis enhances both zygotic and gametic fitness, it drives the allele frequencies of loci linked to Heterosis toward long-term equilibrium values of 0.5. Finally, we explore how to calculate reproductive gains in sexual reproduction, where meiotic drive influences the results. In this scenario, if meiotic bias increases zygotic fitness, natural selection favors a long-term meiotic bias factor of 0.5. This represents another way to operationalize Fisher's "compensation principle." Additionally, we derive the equilibrium conditions for allele frequencies in Heterosis when sexual reproduction is imperfect, and we illustrate how to determine the specific parameters of meiotic bias for X chromosome inheritance in mammals. These findings help explain the observed higher average allele frequencies on X chromosomes in mammals compared to autosomes. Such insights clarify why Heterosis in sexual reproduction can maintain HOGNs (non-ungdominant non-negligible traits) and provide a foundation for updating Fisher's HOGNs based on the principles of meiotic drive. This approach also offers an alternative explanation for the fundamental laws of sexual reproduction in evolutionary genetics, illustrating how the compounding of gametic fitness over multiple generations, influenced by HOGNs in Heterosis, results in HOGN allele frequencies converging to 1 in zygotes. This mechanism helps address the evolutionary origin of DNA replication in sexual reproduction. Additionally, we illustrate how to apply Fisher's second extension to HOGNs in Asexual reproduction and derive the frequency dynamics of HOGNs under this framework. This leads to a new understanding of the HOGNs in the Large Asexual Theory. By integrating HOGNs into the analysis of reproductive rates and asexual inheritance, we establish that HOGNs in the Large Asexual Theory can increase in both quantity and quality through replication. To address this, various FL algorithms have been developed to enhance permutation stability and consistency with local data distributions. While the Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) method offers significant improvements in stability and convergence, it lacks a clear convergence guarantee. Specifically, the gradient variance produced by the locally averaged dataset in PFL does not effectively upper-bound the gradient variance of the global data, hindering precise convergence analysis. This paper presents a novel convergence analysis for PFL under data heterogeneity. We derive an explicit bound for the gradient variance of local data relative to the global average, use this to prove PFL's convergence, and reveal that FL performance degradation scales linearly with the variance of local data. These variance components represent the maximum permutation stability of local datasets. Furthermore, experimental results validate our theoretical analysis, demonstrating that PFL achieves superior stability and convergence compared to other FL algorithms such as FedAvg and FedProx. Finally, to further enhance performance, we introduce a regularization term that mitigates data heterogeneity, resulting in an augmented personalized learning algorithm with guaranteed convergence. These datasets are employed to construct phenomenological and effective field theory models. When applied to observe a merger event with a mass ratio of 0.7 and zero eccentricity using a third-generation advanced interferometer, the phenomenological model predicts a 3.6% uncertainty in the neutron star's tidal deformability, stemming from the uncertainty in the inspiral-spin-quadrupole coefficients of the lighter body. Although intermediate eccentricities or higher mass ratios typically yield larger memory amplitudes, the predominant source of uncertainty remains the tidal deformability of the more massive object across the parameters investigated. This remains the primary bottleneck in extracting neutron star equation-of-state information, even exceeding the uncertainties caused by imperfect phenomenological models of the most advanced and sensitive future detectors, such as Cosmic Explorer or Einstein Telescope. To achieve a 10% precision in tidal deformability, researchers either need to analyze multiple merger events or simultaneously observe gravitational waves and electromagnetic signals from neutron star collisions to constrain system parameters during the extraction of EOS information. Including electromagnetic observations from the merger's collision phase can significantly tighten constraints on tidal deformability for independent events by mass ratios of 0.7 or lower. Consequently, the simultaneous detection of electromagnetic and gravitational signals from neutron star mergers by next-generation advanced interferometers is essential for determining neutron star equations of states, regardless of the specific mass ratio or eccentricity of the colliding objects. This study constitutes the first numerical-relativity analysis of how merger memory influences the extraction of neutron star tidal deformability from gravitational-wave observations of individual events. Subsequent work will examine higher order post-Newtonian parameters, including spin effects, to determine if they can enhance precision. The accompanying software repository offers an example of how to utilize the proposed phenomenological model to conduct similar analyses for other mass ratios, eccentricities, and observational scenarios.

This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings and introduce a generalized stochastic model—encompassing both the analyzed case and several related scenarios—that encourages the development of more precise prior distributions for task difficulties. This model offers intuitive insights into the coordination of rational agents and practical methods for leveraging these insights to enhance the performance of strategic agent teams. The name of this model is INSIDE, which stands for an acronym derived from the reverse of the words "EDNIS" (English for Intelligent Nash Equilibrium with Prior Selection and Diffuse Isotropy). The acronyms also represent the primary contribution of this paper: Agent Teams can BE INSIDE an Easy Linear Equilibrium when Prior Diffuseness is NOT Diffuse. Our results emphasize the significance of domain knowledge in achieving effective coordination among strategic agents. Additionally, the paper includes source code for the algorithms, simulation data, and data collectors required to replicate and extend our research.

This difficulty stems primarily from privacy concerns regarding sensitive organizational data. To address this, we introduce a novel federated learning system that integrates three core components. The first component enables the training of a federated learning model on local organizational data without exposing the underlying information. The second involves aggregating these local models into a robust anomaly detection model with reduced bias, achieved through a new weighted averaging technique that accounts for the varying numbers of under-sampled classes in each local model. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, Behavior Tree Optimization (BTO), designed to reorganize a sub-optimal plan into a better one, or optimize a optimal plan further, while operating within constrained computational resources. Modeled after genetic algorithms, BTO utilizes a behavior tree representation commonly found in robotic control systems. Our approach was validated in a physical environment using the Robotis TAU-ORPHEUS humanoid. Experimental results demonstrate that BTO surpasses existing planning algorithms, such as those based on A* and A3*, across all tested scenarios. Furthermore, by consuming fewer computational resources, the robot can execute additional tasks during the plan optimization process. Given that behavior trees are the industry standard for robot planning, our findings suggest that BTO has broad applicability and can enhance plans for sequences of multi-tasks longer than what current methods can handle.

The demand for cost-effective Wireless Backscatter Communication (WBS) systems has driven extensive research, yet this research has primarily focused on point-to-point (P2P) setups involving a single source and one reflector. In contrast, $N$-tuple WBS communication, which allows $N$ devices to transmit data simultaneously, can significantly boost system throughput and energy efficiency, preparing the technology for next-generation applications. Current literature offers no solutions for energy allocation in $N$-tuple WBS systems, and existing multiple-access algorithms are derived from traditional wireless networks, which backscatter communication cannot directly adopt due to its distinct modulation and energy harvesting mechanisms. This study addresses simultaneous energy allocation for $N$-tuple WBS under a specific multiple access scheme. We formulate an optimization problem to distribute energy among transmitters, aiming to maximize the sum of successful packets received by destinations. Experimental validation using a physical robotic platform confirms that our proposed algorithm outperforms existing schemes in both sum success rates and total energy efficiency. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first energy allocation solution for $N$-tuple WBS. Experimental results indicate that our algorithm achieves a 50% gain in energy efficiency compared to other approaches.

This approach identifies the dynamics that drive systems toward specific manifold, defines a metric to measure proximity to desired synchronization patterns, and assesses the robustness of these patterns against graph structure variations and weight changes. Group synchronization involves multiple synchronization patterns occurring simultaneously in a system of interacting oscillators. While various approaches exist for analyzing such phenomena in specific systems with known interaction structures, there is no general framework that directly links system interactions to the resulting patterns. In this work, we fill this gap by examining the geometry of the solution space for a generalized group synchronization equation (GSE) that models interactions at the group level. We show how to represent the solution space as a union of symmetry-based synchronization manifolds, derive conditions for manifold connectivity, and establish a method to compute the combinatorial distance between patterns. These findings demonstrate how system interactions, even when acting on groups of oscillators, determine the emergence of specific synchronization patterns and their robustness. Additionally, we derive a group synchronization matrix that extends the standard symmetry matrix to accommodate the more general context. This matrix can be used to design control laws for inducing desired synchronizations, identify feasible patterns, and analyze the stability of pattern boundaries. Finally, we illustrate how this group synchronization framework can be effectively applied to address key open challenges in solving symmetry-breaking problems.

The core concept involves connecting $N$ coupled oscillators, each producing signals at distinct frequencies ($f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_N$), where these individual outputs are integer multiples of a base frequency $f_0$ (i.e., $f_i = m_i \cdot f_0$ for $i=2,3,\ldots,N$). Signal generation at these $N$ frequencies is achieved through two distinct architectures: the Multiple Frequency Coupled Oscillator (MFCO) and the Multiple Frequency Cross-Coupled Oscillator (MCCO). The CCOs are linked via cross-coupling, and the specific topology is determined by the sub-harmonic order $f_j / f_i$ where $j > i$. For the MCCO, additional connections are established between every pair of oscillators, resulting in a higher connection density compared to the MFCO. Both oscillator topologies demonstrate frequency robustness within an 800 MHz bandwidth at 500 MHz and 2.4 GHz, exhibiting less than 1% frequency variation under varying process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions. The 2.4 GHz, 190 mW MCCO oscillator, fabricated in a 90 nm CMOS process, occupies an area of 105 $\mu$m$\times$105 $\mu$m, corresponds to 9.5% of the total chip area, and consumes 4.5 mW per generated frequency. This represents a 62.5% reduction in power consumption compared to an equivalent system using $N$ independent, non-overlapping free-running oscillators. Furthermore, per-frequency power usage is reduced by 25% relative to $N$ independent overdriven differential CCOs. To our knowledge, these oscillators operate at the highest recorded frequencies for radio frequency (RF) applications. These findings indicate that multiple coupled oscillator topologies are highly power-efficient, suggesting their potential utility in RF systems such as RF synthesizers, multi-carrier modulation, and cognitive radio. Any solution to the Einstein equations, whether including or excluding a cosmological constant, adheres to the field equations defined by the Cotton tensor, indicating that the cosmological constant functions as an integration constant. In this theoretical framework, a vacuum state is characterized by the vanishing of the Cotton tensor instead of the Ricci tensor. Furthermore, an exact Schwarzschild-like solution for a static, spherically symmetric source has been identified. Despite the field equations originally involving third-order derivatives, a variational principle reveals that they simplify into second-order differential equations. This rescaling relationship enables the formulation of variational principles using the Einstein-Hilbert action. This paper introduces a novel inexact Newton method, which can be seamlessly embedded within an IPM to efficiently calculate search directions for a broad range of linear complementarity problems (LCPs) that possess a cyclic positive index-2 structure. Although it serves as a simple extension of the linear feedback equation, it exhibits rich dynamics, for which numerous studies have explored the dynamics of linear feedback within delay equations. In this work, we present numerical and analytical evidence suggesting a strong analogy between linear and nonlinear feedback mechanisms. Specifically, we examine the impact of the restoring force on the system's dynamics when the parameter is varied. In doing so, we introduce a generalized form of the delayed logistic equation that incorporates linear restoring terms and can be viewed as a discretized version of the van der Pol oscillator. Our findings indicate that the absence of restoring forces is not a unique property of nonlinear delayed logistic equations but is, in fact, a distinct and intriguing feature of the delayed logistic equation itself. Consequently, we conclude that linear and nonlinear damping terms contribute almost identically to the system's overall dynamics, with two notable exceptions: nonlinear damping generates no additional bifurcations, and it fails to produce a unique steady-state solution. Conversely, we observe that linear restoring forces are essential for observing a unique solution within the context of delayed logistic and similar equations. This insight may offer a fresh perspective on the longstanding "paradox" associated with Hutchinson's work. Finally, we discuss the implications of linear restoring forces in other fields and propose this equation as a viable alternative to the original delayed logistic equation.

Recent developments in point process depth have introduced a weighted product of two components: the count of points falling outside an outer depth contour and the maximum distance to this contour. This paper proposes an alternative construction for a significant portion of that outer contour, suggesting that the "maximum distance" component is redundant. In this study, we investigate two pathways to ideal engines: first, quantum systems functioning as hybrid machines capable of executing multiple useful tasks, and second, the reduction of fluctuations during these operations. For classical devices, the elimination of fluctuations requires high entropy production, as mandated by thermodynamic uncertainty relations. We extend these relations to multiterminal conductors operating as hybrid thermal machines. Our results demonstrate that quantum conductors surpass these classical limits, illustrated by a double quantum dot connected to normal metals and a reservoir that generates entangled Cooper pairs. It demonstrates how to generate samples from a distribution proportional to the equilibrium Boltzmann factor, $e^{-\beta U(x)}$, where $\beta$ represents the inverse thermal energy and $U(x)$ denotes the potential energy. The approach is particularly useful for analyzing high-energy landscapes, such as the cost functions of complex systems, by averaging over the corresponding thermal distributions. In this specific example, the potential $U(x)$ corresponds to the generalized Rayleigh (GM) energy, $\sum_k |x_k-x_{k+1}|^2$, which is commonly employed to evaluate one-dimensional denoising algorithms like denoising autoencoders. The potential energy is defined as a sum of local components, $U(x) = \sum_k U_k(x)$, where $U_k$ relies exclusively on the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-th variables. Equipped with the ability to compute the derivative of these local potentials, we can construct a stochastic thermodynamic integration (TTI) method to draw samples from the Boltzmann distribution. The method begins by generating initial samples from a distribution $P_0$, which may differ from the target Boltzmann distribution. These samples are organized into a Markov chain, and at each step, a uniform random index $k$ is selected to propose a new state, $x'_{k}$. The new state accepts with a probability defined by a specific formula. To ensure a valid Markov chain, the index selection must be uniform; while a random number of indices can reduce the dimensionality of the stationary distribution, it risks breaking the Markov property, particularly in small systems. Additionally, the choice of a specific index does not impact the method's asymptotic performance, as all local potentials contribute equivalently to the total energy in the limit of large $N$. Consequently, the method remains effective for the system sizes typically handled by this tutorial. A critical challenge in this sampling framework is balancing the acceptance probability. If the factor $\beta\Delta U$ in the formula is excessively large, the proposed states will frequently be rejected, whereas a very small value may result in nearly universal rejections, effectively reducing the method to a random walker in such extreme scenarios. Meanwhile, the nature of social connections evolves as agents join or leave friendships if the discrepancy between their views exceeds a specific threshold. Consistent with the broader social balance framework, agents are categorized as friends or foes, and links between foes automatically become negative, signifying disapproval. Numerical simulations analyze a single-agent system involving a positive-minded leader (friendly to most) and a negative-minded minority, demonstrating how opinion dispersion stabilizes depending on the strength of disapproval held by the minority toward the majority. Additionally, we present specific initial configurations that generate a wide range of steady-state opinion distributions. Finally, we investigate these dynamics in a larger system featuring multiple ideological camps, each characterized by a high-ranking leader and a supportive entourage. These camps exchange negative evaluations of the opposing camps among their friends, creating a network primarily composed of intra-camp ties that are mostly positive, thereby fostering conflict between different ideological groups. We then investigate how these network dynamics evolve over a prolonged timescale, specifically when the propensity to form bounded-confidence opinions and to revise social links is very low, preventing the rapid evolution of individual agent traits and network topology. In this regime, the system can settle into steady states where positive and negative edges are approximately evenly distributed, achieving global social balance, or into periodically oscillating states where these edges fluctuate. We demonstrate that both equilibrium and oscillating patterns can emerge from diverse initial conditions. Notably, the system can transition from a socially balanced equilibrium to oscillations, or vice versa, via a limit cycle. Equilibrium social balance is more likely when the network begins in a balanced configuration. Conversely, the system tends toward oscillations when starting in a network where social triples are mostly anti-balanced. When social balance is not achieved, we calculate the density of anti-balanced social triples across various scenarios. In the final equilibrium state, we observe that the density of negative disapproval among differing opinions remains low, thereby minimizing the impact of disapproval on the distribution of opinion differences in steady states. These systems stabilize in a bistable regime, where the resulting opinion distribution depends on the initial configuration. We conclude that opinion formation within ideological camps, reinforced by negative evaluations of opposing camps, produces strongly bistable opinion distributions. Consequently, this mechanism helps explain how opinion distributions can becomepolarized and how it becomes difficult to reverse deeply polarized individual opinions. IOP Publishing. 2022.

The Cell Functional Definition of Cancer Mitosis and the Cancer Phenome: A Temporal Model of Cancer as a Distinct Entity

Abstract

While genes with similar transcriptional activation kinetics may display vastly different mRNA timelines, these discrepancies arise from differences in transcription and processing durations, as well as post-transcriptional mechanisms. Therefore, cells with varying genomic architectures are anticipated to exhibit different mRNA timelines, despite having identical gene regulation patterns. This study suggests that such structural differences are the cause of the diverse temporal expression patterns found in cancer cells. The model described here, which is supported by a substantial array of experimental data, serves a dual purpose: it provides a functional definition of cancer mitosis and helps establish a temporal understanding of cancer as a distinct entity, known as the Cancer Phenome. Additionally, the model indicates that cell cycle and other cellular functions are expected to inﬂuence many gene expression timelines, creating discrepancies between tumor cells and normal cells. This model provides a rationale for the functional definitions of mitotic interphase and mitosis. Furthermore, it supports the diagnosis and therapy of cancer by offering a way to measure cancer as a distinct entity, with mRNA timelines serving as its biochemical markers. Keywords: Gene regulation, time, cancer, model, phenotype, mitosis, cell cycle, chemotherapy, diagnosis, therapy.

In many computer vision tasks, such as person or animal recognition, datasets are often unbalanced, lacking sufficient examples for classification. In object tracking, a similar issue arises due to the constant introduction of new classes. To address this, researchers have explored generating synthetic classes from existing data to expand training sets. However, current generation methods typically produce only visual features, neglecting auxiliary modalities like sound. This work introduces the Sound-Augment method, which expands a dataset by generating new classes accompanied by their corresponding sounds. The approach applies style transfer between images and sounds to translate visual-acoustic pairs into sounds of target classes. A key advantage is that the method does not require prior knowledge of the sounds for the new classes. Additionally, we present an auditory-discriminative augmentation strategy where the method uses existing class sounds to generate sounds of target classes. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently enhances the performance of visual acoustics. Public code and data are available at https://github.com/davidbkr/sound-augment.

This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of algorithmic biases affecting information retrieval, and the extent of relevant data potentially lost due to personalization. This study builds upon and extends our previous work [1], which developed a method to reduce the complexity of quantum many-body models by separating spatial and spin degrees of freedom. In the current paper, we apply this approach to Heisenberg-type models, demonstrating its validity across a broad range of interactions. We also explore the method's relevance to spin-orbit coupled systems.

Starting from a tight-binding model for electrons on a lattice, we derive an effective Hamiltonian that retains only spin degrees of freedom. This is achieved by constructing and solving the equation of motion for orbital degrees of freedom in their steady state. Subsequently, we eliminate quadrupole terms from the effective Hamiltonian under conditions of strong spin-orbit coupling. Our findings indicate that these effective Hamiltonians, which are generally non-exchange symmetric, are well-suited for numerical simulations using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger method [2]. As an illustration, we analyze a model with easy-plane anisotropy on a bipartite lattice, demonstrating a phase transition at a specific coupling constant value.

We introduce a novel class of integrable Hamiltonians featuring chiral and spin-orbit coupling, derived from the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. These Hamiltonians exhibit a rich phase diagram characterized by topological and symmetry-protected symmetry breaking phases. We provide a complete analytical classification of this phase diagram and utilize our methodology to determine the critical points for a broad range of spin-orbit coupling strengths. Specifically, we derive an exact expression for the critical line separating polar and ferromagnetic phases, which shows a non-trivial dependence on the spin-orbit coupling parameter. Furthermore, we analytically calculate the order parameter for the transition into the ferromagnetic phase and empirically validate our findings by comparing theoretical predictions for the order parameter with results from a systematic finite-size scaling analysis.

We also empirically investigate the dynamical response of the system, analyzing the temporal evolution of local magnetization following a sudden quench of the spin-orbit coupling strength. This data provides a theoretical framework for experimentally observing quantum phase transitions in cold-atom systems.

The optical and near-infrared follow-up of the resulting kilonova—the ejected material from such mergers—provided the first evidence that heavy nuclei are synthesized via the rapid neutron capture process (r-process) in these astrophysical environments. Since the emission of optical and near-infrared radiation from a kilonova is driven by the radiative energy released from ejecta containing r-process elements, this radiation curve offers a valuable instrument for identifying and locating these mergers. Over the last five years, as gravitational wave and optical/infrared detection capabilities have improved, so too has our understanding of r-process elements within kilonovae. These advancements enable us to measure the masses and orbital separations of merging double-stellar systems, as the initial parameters of the binary dictate the characteristics of the ejected material. Furthermore, the detection of r-process elements in planetary nebulae has been made possible, providing a method to estimate the historical production of heavy elements, trace galactic chemical evolution, and investigate the formation environments of r-process nuclei. Additionally, these observations have significantly reduced the uncertainty surrounding the origin of r-process elements once attributed to unidentified sources. Today, confirmed kilonova observations stand as the most robust proof that heavy nuclei are produced in violent astrophysical events, a finding that has sparked intense interest in the astrophysical settings capable of generating such extreme conditions. In this thesis, I present a review of the current state of research regarding kilonovae, their r-process elements, and the resulting implications for astrophysics. This work also introduces a novel model of a kilonova's expanding ejecta, offering a standardization of future simulations with established parameters. Finally, I propose that the variability in observed kilonova light curves may be more closely linked to post-ejection phenomena, such as the interaction between the expanding material and a surrounding envelope, rather than varying orbital separations or the specific properties of the r-process itself. This research area remains highly active, with new findings emerging regularly that hold significant potential for the field. By utilizing MR-Linacs, which combine magnetic resonance imaging with linear accelerators, oncologists can visualize tumor positions in real-time and deliver precise radiation doses that account for daily variations in tumor cell presence. Currently, manually outlining the stomach and intestines to adjust beam directions for safe dose delivery is a time-consuming and labor-intensive task. To streamline this workflow, this paper introduces a deep learning-based data augmentation method that leverages intra-treatment images to enhance inter-treatment imaging for anatomical segmentation. Our approach utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network to generate synthetic tumors and organs representing inter-treatment distributions, based on the frequent tumors seen during treatment. Subsequently, a generative style-transfer technique is employed to style these synthetic organs to match the inter-treatment distribution of the target patient. Finally, these conditioned synthetic organs are utilized to train a convolutional neural network, enabling the segmentation of new patient tumors. To our knowledge, this represents the first deep learning-based data augmentation and segmentation methodology that can be directly applied to clinical settings. Experimental results on real patient data indicate that this approach can reduce daily treatment times by approximately 10 minutes or more. Additionally, we developed a new evaluation metric to assess the performance of this condition-to-inter transformation method. This work demonstrates that advanced AI can facilitate the development of personalized medicine by adapting general models to individual patients. By leveraging data collected during treatment, our method allows for the most accurate identification of tumors relative to organs at risk, thereby supporting the vision of personalized medicine. This advancement holds significant potential for creating a more efficient and cost-effective healthcare system. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhangyiqi2000/CLITGAN.

This noise affects high-frequency radial velocity data and can masquerade as planetary signals with periods under 10 days, making it impossible to rule out short-period planets using this dataset alone. Reanalyzing the data with a modified upper limit for TIP noise reveals that the number of detectable short-period planets would more than double, S4 would rise by 1.8 m/s, and the minimum mass of Earth-size planets with a 200-day orbit would drop to 1.5 Earth masses.
